tier_reason: First-party harness (cpp/benchmarks/bench_psio_vs_externals.cpp, adapters under cpp/benchmarks/adapters/) states llvm-clang 22.1 and -O3 -DNDEBUG, but hardware is only 'Apple M-series' with no CPU model, canonical-library versions are not given, and the anchor CSV sits under /tmp and is not committed. There is no independent suite or paper, so this is C, not B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Geomean latency ratios vs pssz (format time / pssz time, psio_bench_vs_externals snapshot, >1 means pssz faster). Decode: protobuf 6.36x, capnp 5.38x, msgpack 18.67x, flatbuf 1.23x. Encode: protobuf 43.40x, capnp 81.96x, flatbuf 57.28x, msgpack 33.38x. View: capnp 47.57x, flatbuf 2.29x. Validate: protobuf 48.01x, flatbuf 8.45x, capnp 6.12x, msgpack 28.76x, but the validate column uses psio's own in-tree implementations of those formats, not the canonical libraries. Size: avro 0.56x, msgpack 0.61x, protobuf 0.65x of pssz, so the varint formats are smaller on the wire. Cumulative geomean: protobuf 12.64x, capnp 10.55x, msgpack 10.23x, flatbuf 5.13x.
corrections.workload: Per-shape geomean of size, encode, decode, validate and view_one latency across reflected struct shapes (Point, NameRecord, FlatRecord, Record, Validator, Order, ValidatorList and bounded variants, plus realistic shapes). Size, encode, decode and view use the canonical libprotobuf, libcapnp, libflatbuffers and msgpack-cxx. Validate always uses psio's own implementations of those formats because the canonical libraries have no comparable validate entry point.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark. Hardware is given only as 'Apple M-series', and versions of the canonical libraries are not stated. The anchor snapshot CSV (/tmp/psio_bench_snap_xx/perf_20260501T081915Z_4b7ae98.csv) is not committed, although commit 4b7ae98 exists. Validate ratios compare pssz against psio's re-implementations of protobuf, flatbuf and capnp, not the canonical libraries. The prose and table disagree slightly: flatbuf validate is 8.64x in the prose and 8.45x in the table, and ssz cumulative is 1.13 in the prose and 1.10 in the table. The repo has no LICENSE file: the Rust crate and npm package manifests declare MIT, the C++ core has no license, and docs/compatibility.md lists supplying license files as pending. 0 stars; version 0.1.0 is pre-release. fracpack is deprecated in favour of pssz in this repo.

notes: The numbers match docs/format-comparison.md exactly, and the benchmark source is public. The only reasons this is not tier A are the missing CPU model and first-party provenance. The record's metric 'throughput' is really latency ratios (ns per op) plus size, and metric is not a correctable field. license stays null because GitHub reports none and there is no LICENSE file, even though the manifests declare MIT.

tier_reason: The numbers come from author-run forks of external suites (fastserial/cpp-serialization-benchmark, fastserial/simdjson, fastserial/kostya-benchmark). Each fork has public code, but the Lite³ author wrote the adapters, and no upstream suite includes Lite³. Only the Cista++ fork names a compiler (g++-11, CMake Release). No CPU model is stated anywhere, and the 242x figure exceeds 50x, so this stays at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Cista++ cpp-serialization-benchmark fork, graph with 1870 nodes: serialize+deserialize takes 7.79 ms for the Lite³ Buffer API vs 1887.49 ms for FlatBuffers (242x, derived from page data; this is the project's '242x'). Serialize is 3.02 vs 1845.8 ms (611x, derived), deserialize/verify 4.77 vs 41.69 ms (8.7x, derived) and traverse 79.39 vs 90.53 ms (1.14x, derived). Message size is 38.069 MB vs 62.998 MB. zpp::bits (4.66 ms) and Cista++ offset slim (3.96 ms) beat Lite³ on serialize+deserialize. The 'up to 120x' claim is simdjson On-Demand find_tweet at 53937 ns vs 448 ns for the Lite³ Buffer API (120x, derived) on twitter.json. In that test Lite³ queries data pre-converted to its binary format while the other libraries parse JSON.
corrections.workload: Three external suites, forked and run by the Lite³ author and linked from the README. (1) Cista++ cpp-serialization-benchmark: serialize, deserialize and traverse a node/edge graph, vs FlatBuffers, Cap'n Proto, cereal, zpp::bits and Cista++. (2) simdjson bench_ondemand queries on twitter.json (~632 kB): top_tweet, partial_tweets, find_tweet and distinct_user_id, vs simdjson, yyjson and RapidJSON, with Lite³ on pre-converted binary data. (3) kostya/benchmarks JSON coordinate sum (~115 MB). The lite3 repo has no harness of its own.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Cista++ fork: g++-11 with CMake Release for the benchmark; liblite3 is built by its Makefile default (-O2 -DNDEBUG). The simdjson and kostya forks state no compiler or flags.
corrections.caveats: All numbers are author-run on forks of external suites, with no CPU model stated. The 242x figure is serialize-dominated: the upstream FlatBuffers adapter builds per-edge tables through a std::map lookup, while the Lite³ adapter memcpys pre-flattened index-based edge arrays as opaque byte blobs. Deserialize is only 8.7x faster and traverse is about equal. zpp::bits and Cista++ offset slim beat Lite³ on serialize+deserialize. The 120x JSON comparisons pit JSON parsing against queries on data already converted to Lite³, so they are not like-for-like. The upstream Cista suite (felixguendling, 37 stars) does not include Lite³.

notes: The record said there was no reproducible harness, but the README links three public benchmark forks with raw output files, so benchmark_url now points at the README Benchmarks section. The tier stays C. The headline 242x and 120x ratios are real on the pages but are derived from uneven comparisons, and claimed_speedup now spells that out. Metadata checks out: MIT, 807 stars, last commit 2026-08-06, active.

tier_reason: Upgraded from stronger evidence: the independent kostya/benchmarks suite (~2.9k stars) runs gason against RapidJSON. Its code is json/test_gason.cpp, json/test_rapid.cpp and common/commands.mk. It states g++ 16.1.0 and clang++ 22.1.8, flags -O3 -march=native -flto=auto, and CPU Intel Xeon E-2324G. gason measured 0.127 s vs 0.154 s for RapidJSON. The first-party README shootout alone would only be C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: kostya/benchmarks JSON test (README update 2026-07-19): gason 0.127 s vs RapidJSON 0.154 s with g++ (1.21x, derived from page data), and 0.133 s vs 0.194 s with clang++ (1.46x, derived). RapidJSON Precise with g++ takes 0.212 s. gason trails simdjson On-Demand (0.060 s), DAW JSON Link (0.089 s) and simdjson DOM (0.107 s), and roughly ties yyjson (0.131 s). The first-party README shootout (2013-14, i7 2.3 GHz, clang-500.2.79) gives gason 924 us vs RapidJSON 2210 us parse on monster.json (2.4x, derived) and 75 vs 91 us on data.json (1.2x, derived), but RapidJSON is faster on big.json (18093 vs 20092 us).
corrections.workload: kostya/benchmarks JSON test: parse a large generated JSON file of 3D coordinates and average the x/y/z values, using idiomatic library code, reported as the median of runs with data loading not timed. The README shootout parses and sums the numbers in big.json, monster.json and data.json.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: kostya/benchmarks: g++ 16.1.0 and clang++ 22.1.8 (-stdlib=libc++), -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -std=c++23. README shootout: clang-500.2.79 (OSX) and gcc 4.8.2 (Android). The page states no flags; the May-2014 CMakeLists (commit add97a2) sets -O3.
corrections.hardware: kostya/benchmarks: Intel Xeon E-2324G (Debian forky/sid Docker image). README shootout: Intel Core i7 2.3 GHz (OSX 10.9) and Samsung Galaxy Note II GT-N7100 (Android 4.3).
corrections.caveats: The independent win over RapidJSON is modest (1.21x with g++, 1.46x with clang++). gason loses to simdjson and DAW JSON Link. kostya notes that gason mutates its input and has number-parsing inaccuracies (vivkin/gason#35); default RapidJSON has the same caveat. The README shootout is from 2013-14 against 2013 RapidJSON svn trunk and gives mixed results, with RapidJSON winning big.json on OSX. Its harness (parser-shootout.cpp, clone-enemy-parsers.sh) was removed from HEAD in Nov 2014 and survives only in git history, and the README build steps reference files that no longer exist. Last commit was 2021-10-18.

notes: The tier is upgraded from B to A on the independent kostya/benchmarks suite, and benchmark_url now points there. The README numbers match the record, but on their own they are first-party and would be C. Metadata checks out: MIT, 339 stars, last commit 2021-10-18, abandoned.
